summary: Describes the queries a DNS resolver should send to initialize its cache, getting the root NS RRset and the root server addresses. It is a BCP. Replaced by RFC 9609.

eli5.summary: A new resolver starts knowing nothing, so it asks who the top servers are.

questions: how does a resolver find root servers
what is a dns priming query
subtitle: How resolvers find the root servers when they start.

tldr.problem: Recursive DNS resolvers need a way to initialize their cache and find the root servers to answer queries.
tldr.mechanism: A resolver sends a priming query (QNAME="." and QTYPE=NS) to one of its configured root server addresses. The response provides the current list of root servers and their addresses.
tldr.outcome: Resolvers can keep their root server list up to date even as servers change addresses, rather than relying on outdated static configuration. This was replaced by RFC 9609.

today: RFC 8109 is a Best Current Practice, but it has been obsoleted by RFC 9609, which provides updated guidance on DNS priming queries.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Recursive DNS resolvers start with an empty cache and need a way to begin resolving queries. The common approach is to configure the resolver with the names and addresses of root servers, then use those to query for an authoritative list of root servers.

The key insight is that resolvers should get the current root server list from the DNS itself, not just from static configuration. Configuration can become out of date as root servers change addresses. Since root server addresses have changed over time for both IPv4 and IPv6, keeping configuration fresh requires resolvers to do priming queries.
sections.eli5: Resolvers start with a list of root servers from the vendor. But instead of just using that list forever, they ask a root server for the official, up-to-date list.

sections.title: The Priming Query
sections.content:
A priming query is a normal DNS query with QNAME="." (the root zone) and QTYPE=NS (requesting the NS records for the root). It is sent over UDP or TCP to one of the configured root server addresses, using a randomly selected source port for UDP.

Resolvers SHOULD use EDNS(0) (see RFC 6891) and announce a reassembly size of at least 1024 octets, since a complete response with all 13 root servers and their addresses can exceed the original 512-octet limit. The Recursion Desired (RD) bit may be set to 0 or 1.
sections.eli5: The query is straightforward: "What are the NS records for the root?" The resolver sends it over the network to a root server and waits for the answer.

sections.title: When to Prime
sections.content:
A resolver SHOULD send a priming query when needed, such as when it starts with an empty cache or when the root zone's NS RRset expires. Because NS records have a TTL like any other record, resolvers should expire them according to that TTL. Resolvers MAY pre-fetch the NS RRset before it expires to keep the cache fresh.

If a priming query fails to get a response, the resolver SHOULD retry with a different root server address from its configuration. To spread the load, resolvers SHOULD randomly select the target address for each priming query rather than always using the same one.
sections.eli5: The resolver does this when it starts or when the list ages out. If one root server doesn't answer, it tries another.

sections.title: The Priming Response
sections.content:
A priming response is a normal DNS response. The resolver expects an RCODE of NOERROR and the Authoritative Answer (AA) bit to be set. The response contains an NS RRset in the Answer section (the root's NS records) and an Additional section with A and AAAA records for each root server.

Resolver software SHOULD treat the priming response like any other DNS response and feed it into its cache. There are currently 13 root servers, each with IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. Not all responses include every server's address due to the size constraint, so resolvers may need to issue follow-up queries for any missing address records.
sections.eli5: The response is just a normal DNS answer saying "Here are the 13 root servers" with their IP addresses.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Spoofing a priming query response can redirect all queries from a resolver to attacker-controlled servers. An on-path attacker seeing a priming query can inject false answers before a real root server responds, poisoning the resolver's cache.

Until priming responses are protected with DNSSEC, there is no definitive way to prevent such redirection. A validating resolver with a trust anchor for the root can detect attacks on the root itself (because root answers are signed), but cannot protect unsigned zones. If the root-servers.net zone were signed, having the DNSSEC OK bit set in priming queries would add protection.
sections.eli5: An attacker could pretend to be a root server and give a fake answer, tricking the resolver. DNSSEC can help prevent this, but only if the zones are signed.
